Pāṇini 1.3.67: *ṇeraṇau yatkarma ṇau cetsa kartānādhyāne*.

The meaning of the sūtra is: the Ātmanepada suffix shall occur after a causative (*ṇic*) verb, provided that the very action which was expressed by the non-causative (*aṇ*) root is expressed by the causative, and the factor which was the object (*karman*) in the non-causative becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative, except in the case of the act of remembering (*ādhyāna*).
II. The scope for the application of the *sūtra*:

Although [the ātmanepada] is already established by the rule "after a causative suffix (*ṇic*)," this [present rule] is for the purpose of [including cases where the action] does not benefit the agent.

However, when the action does benefit the agent, since the option provided by "optionally [when there is] a co-occurring word (*upapada*)" would apply, and since the parasmaipada provided by "after a root that is not intransitive (*aṇāv akarmakāt*)" would also apply by virtue of being a subsequent rule, this very [present rule] is intended [to prevail] through the principle of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

Verbs whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*) and verbs whose activity resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*) are the examples. III. The manner of applying the definition to the object of observation (the *lakṣya*).
III. 1. The manner of applying the definition to a verbal root whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*), according to the view that the instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇapakṣa*).
The purpose of the third sentence in the sutra is explained as follows: "The devotees see Bhava" means they make him the object of visual cognition (*cākṣuṣajñāna*).

When the causal element (*preraṇā*) is set aside, it becomes "Bhava sees," meaning he becomes the object. Then, with the causative suffix *ṇic* added for that reason, it becomes "the devotees cause Bhava to be seen," which means they see him.
Furthermore, when the sense of causation (*ṇyartha*) is not intended to be expressed, [the form] *darśayate bhavaḥ* occurs.

Here, the meaning is identical in the first and third stages, as well as in the second and fourth. In that regard, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffix does not occur in the third stage; although there is equality of action (*kriyāsāmya*), the agent (*kartṛ*) of the root in the causative (*ṇau*) is not the same as the object (*karmakāraka*) of the non-causative (*aṇau*). However, in the fourth stage, *taṅ* does occur because there is equality of action relative to the second stage, and because the object (*karman*) in the first stage—namely, *bhava*—is here the agent (*kartṛ*). III. 2. Regarding the manner of application when the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyaka*) in a verbal root under the view of the "withdrawal of instigation" (*nivṛttapreṣaṇapakṣa*): *ārohayate hastī* ("the elephant causes himself to be mounted") is also an example.
The elephant-keepers mount the elephant; the meaning is that they cause it to bend down.
Thereafter, the elephant mounts; the meaning is that it bends down.
Thereafter, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), "they cause to mount"; the meaning is "they mount."

Then, it is caused to ascend; the meaning is that it becomes downward-facing. III. 3. Regarding the case where the state (bhāva) resides in the agent and the action (kriyā) resides in the agent, under the view that the instigation (preṣaṇa) is superimposed, the manner of the desired syntactic connection and the purpose of the second sentence in the Sūtra are as follows: or rather, they see [it thus]: "they ascend" is the first stage, as before. Then, because the object itself is superimposed with the status of being the cause (hetu), the causative suffix (ṇic) is applied: *darśayati bhavaḥ* ("Bhava causes [them] to see"), *ārohayati hastī* ("the elephant causes [them] to ascend"). The meaning is that he instigates those who are seeing and those who are ascending.

Then, when both causative operations (*preṣaṇa*)—those expressed by the suffixes *ṇic* and *śānac*, as well as those inherent in their respective bases—are abandoned, the examples are *darśayate* and *ārohayate*. The meaning is as before. In this view, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings do not occur in the second stage (*kakṣyā*), because there is an absence of "identical action" (*samānakriyatva*) due to the addition of the meaning of the *ṇic* suffix. IV. The purpose of the word *anādhyāne* (except for the sense of "remembering with longing") found in the Sūtra is as follows: [The examples would follow here. In the case of *paśyati devadatto rājānam* ("Devadatta sees the king"), when the agent of seeing is made the object by the *ṇic* suffix, it becomes *darśayati devadatto rājānam* ("Devadatta causes the king to see [himself]"). When the *ṇic* suffix is subsequently dropped, the form remains *darśayati*. Here, the meaning of the *ṇic* suffix is not entirely absent; rather, the causal operation (*preṣaṇa*) is suppressed. Therefore, since the action is not identical, the *taṅ* ending does not apply. This is the purpose of the phrase *anādhyāne*. Similarly, in the case of *ārohati hastī sthalam* ("The elephant climbs onto dry land"), when the agent of climbing is made the object by the *ṇic* suffix, it becomes *ārohayati hastī svayameva* ("The elephant causes itself to climb"). When the *ṇic* suffix is subsequently dropped, the form remains *ārohayati*. Here too, the meaning of the *ṇic* suffix is not entirely absent; rather, the causal operation is suppressed. Therefore, since the action is not identical, the *taṅ* ending does not apply. This is the purpose of the phrase *anādhyāne*. However, in the case of *smarati vanagulmaś cātakān* ("The thicket of forest trees remembers the cātakas"), when the agent of remembering is made the object by the *ṇic* suffix, it becomes *smārayati vanagulmaś cātakān svayameva* ("The thicket of forest trees causes itself to be remembered"). When the *ṇic* suffix is subsequently dropped, the form remains *smārayati*. Here, the meaning of the *ṇic* suffix is not entirely absent; rather, the causal operation is suppressed. However, because the action is identical, the *taṅ* ending applies. This is the purpose of the phrase *anādhyāne*. Furthermore, in the case of *paśyati devadatto rājānam* ("Devadatta sees the king"), when the agent of seeing is made the object by the *ṇic* suffix, it becomes *darśayate devadatto rājñā* ("Devadatta causes himself to be seen by the king"). When the *ṇic* suffix is subsequently dropped, the form remains *darśayate*. Here, the meaning of the *ṇic* suffix is not entirely absent; rather, the causal operation is suppressed. However, because the action is identical, the *taṅ* ending applies. This is the purpose of the phrase *anādhyāne*. When the *ṇic* suffix is subsequently dropped, the form remains *ārohayate*. Here too, the meaning of the *ṇic* suffix is not entirely absent; rather, the causal operation is suppressed. What is the purpose of excluding *adhyāna* (thinking/intense reflection)? [In the sentence] "The cuckoo remembers the forest thicket" (*smarati vanagulmaṃ kokilaḥ*), [the passive form] "the forest thicket causes [him] to remember" (*smarayati vanagulmaḥ*) is not valid. The meaning is that [the object] becomes the focus of a memory preceded by longing (*utkaṇṭhā*). According to the view of Bhaṭṭoji [Dīkṣita], the meaning of the sūtra, along with examples and counter-examples, has been explained here up to the word "syāt" under the heading "ṇeḥ" in the *Prakriyā-prakāśa*, following the *Prauḍhamanoramā*. Specifically, the rule states: "When there is no *adhyāna*, that which is the object (*karman*) of the root in the *ṇic*-less state, if it is also the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *ṇic*-inflected state, then the *ṇic* takes the *ātmanepada* endings. * **Example:** *paṭhati pāṭhayati* ("He studies / He causes [himself] to study"). * **Counter-example:** *paṭhati pāṭhayati śiṣyaṃ guruḥ* ("The teacher makes the student study")—here the object of the *ṇic*-less verb is not the agent of the *ṇic*-inflected one. * **Counter-example:** *paṭhati pāṭhayate śiṣyeṇa guruḥ* ("The teacher causes the student to study")—here the object of the *ṇic*-less verb is not the agent of the *ṇic*-inflected one. * **Counter-example:** *paṭhati pāṭhayate śiṣyaḥ svayameva* ("The student studies and causes himself to study")—this is excluded because it involves *adhyāna* (intense reflection/self-study). Thus, the rule is established to ensure the *ātmanepada* suffixes apply only when the object of the base verb becomes the agent of the causative, provided no intense reflection is involved. This concludes the section on the application of the rule.

The rule *aṇau yatkarma ṇau cet* constitutes a separate sentence. Here, the word *karma* refers to "action," as in the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*. This is explained by the phrase: "if that very action which [was] in the *aṇ* [is present] in the *ṇ*" (*aṇau yā kriyā saiva cet*). The word *kartṛ* forms another sentence; the portion beginning with *aṇau* and ending with the word *cet* is understood here by way of ellipsis. Furthermore, the word *karma* here refers to a specific grammatical factor (*kāraka*), since this is based on the governing context of technical terminology (*śabdādhikāra*). This is explained by the passage beginning with *aṇau yat*.

He explains the portion beginning with *anādhyāne* as "but not" (*na tu*). It has been explained that in this context, a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is not particularly faulty; however, one should not be dogmatic about it. This is because an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*) is more logical, and because there is no contradiction with the intended meaning (*lakṣya*). [Commentary] Regarding *ṇeraṇau*:

the phrase "intent on action" (*kriyāpara*) is used because, according to the subsequent sentence, the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) is prescribed for that which was the object (*karman*) when the suffix *ṇiC* is not present (*aṇau*). This is the underlying intention.

If it is argued that, since the word *karman* refers to "action" (*kriyā*), the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* should have been formulated immediately before *ṇeraṇau anādhyāne*—the meaning of the sūtra being that in a *ṇic*-formed verb, the agent whose action is identical to the action residing in the object of the base verb (*aṇau*) is treated like an object (*karmavat*)—we say no; for this would result in the application of the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment as well. The phrase *saiva cet* (if that very same [action]... implies the restriction "only" (*eva*) by the force of the context. For even if there is an addition of something further in the second stage (*kakṣyā*) involving superimposed instigation (*adhyāropita-preṣaṇa*), the existence of that [original action] remains unimpaired; otherwise, the entire statement would become redundant.

Regarding the phrase "it follows" (*anuvartate*): although it was stated in the *Bhāṣya* on *iko guṇavṛddhī* (P. 1.1.3) that there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) when there is a connection with *ey*, nevertheless, the intention here is that a connection does occur because there is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), due to the force of the *svarita* accent, and due to the requirement of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Regarding the phrase "by the prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*): the proof for this is shown by the example from the *Bhāṣya*: *rājā*. [The rule] *aṇāvakarmakāt* (P. 1.3.88) would apply; the intention is that [the root] becomes intransitive (*akarmaka*) through the cessation of the instigation (*nivṛttapreṣaṇatva*).
Raising the objection that this sūtra is already covered by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), he says: "The state [bhāva] resides in the agent," and so forth.

A "state" (*bhāva*) is that which is accomplished by means of an instrument that does not involve physical motion; "action" (*kriyā*) is that which is accomplished by means of an instrument involving physical motion. The point is that the extension (*atideśa*) expressed as "like the object" (*karmavat*) applies only to states residing in the object and actions residing in the object, and not to others; this is what will be established as the final doctrine (*siddhānta*).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "an example from the Bhāṣya": one should not say that this usage in the Bhāṣya occurs when the fruit of the action goes to another (*paragāmitve*). For it must be stated that even when the fruit of the action goes to the agent (*kartṛgāmini*), there is no obstacle to the application of the rule *aṇāvakarmake* (Pāṇini 1.3.88), since it is subsequent (*paratvāt*). This is because its application is unavoidable due to its being subsequent even when the fruit goes to another, as it is necessary for that purpose. The point is that the term *kartrabhiprāye* does not carry over (*anuvartate*) there, because of the absence of a fruit [in that case].

Nor should it be argued that, because the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.88) is established by grammatical tradition (*vyutpatti*) as having its application restricted to the delimiting property of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), the status of being intransitive is understood here only as delimited by the state of being in the *aṇ*-ending form; consequently, [the prohibition] does not apply here, since even the sentence "he sees the king" (*rājānaṃ paśyati*) possesses that state of being in the *aṇ*-ending form. This is because [the restriction] is accepted in order to prevent the misconception of a coreferential application (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Such is the underlying intention.

It should be understood that when there is a firm mental conviction regarding the application of this very rule in the domain of Pāṇini’s sūtra *vibhāṣopapadena* (1.3.77), then in that specific domain, it is indeed based on a formal scriptural statement (*vācanika*).

He says "aparispanda" (non-vibratory) because, otherwise, the terms *bhāva* (state/activity) and *kriyā* (action) would be seen as synonyms. Therein, he provides an example of a verb where the state resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*) with the words "paśyanti" and so forth. The root *dṛś* (to see) denotes the act of causing an object to become the secondary object of a specific cognition; for it is necessary that transitive roots denote two distinct parts [the action and the result]. According to the established doctrine, the agent is the substratum of the operation expressed by the verbal root, while the object is that which possesses the fruit expressed by the root as being non-co-located with that operation. He states this very point with the words "cākṣuṣa" and so forth.

"Instigation" (*preraṇā*)—the sense is that this is intended to express ease of performance. "Bhava sees"—this is the present tense (*laṭ*) in the active voice (*kartari*). And it has been said: "When the instigation ceases, the object remains situated within its own constituent action; as its status as an object (*karmatva*) ceases, it persists in its own status as an agent (*kartṛtva*)."

[Commentary] *Viṣayatvāpādanam* (the bringing about of the state of being an object): an operation conducive to the attainment of the state of being an object. *“Aṃśadvaye” (in two parts)*: the meaning is that it consists of the form of both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). Nor is there an inconsistency in its being cited as an example on the grounds that in the fourth stage (*kakṣyā*) it denotes only the result, because the part consisting of the operation (*kriyā*) in the base root (*aṇau*) would be absent; for in that case, it is the meaning of the verbal root itself that is grasped by the word "operation" (*kriyā*). Alternatively, even there, there is the cognition of an operation coreferential with that [result]; thus, the phrase “in two parts” means “in two parts that are not coreferential. *Nivṛttapreṣaṇam* (with the instigation ceased): that which has abandoned the instigation and is the substratum of the result of the verbal root's meaning.

"In its own action-component" (*svakriyāvayave*): the meaning is that [the object] resides by way of being a locus (*ādheyatayā*) within a portion of what is denoted by the verbal root—namely, the result (*phala*) which determines the status of being the object residing in itself, or the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is co-locus with that result. "While it ceases to exist" (*nivartamāne*): the sense is that there is an absence of being the locus of a result that is non-co-locus with the operation expressed by the verbal root under discussion.

"It remains" (*avatiṣṭhate*): the sense is that it rests upon the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which constitutes the primary element. Since the extended application (*atideśa*) of "like the object" (*karmavat*) does not apply here, the suffixes *śaP* and so on occur according to the rules for an agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*). Therefore, its form is identical to that of the pure agent (*kartṛ*). The word "from that" (*tataḥ*) refers to the root *dṛś*, because its function consists merely in the attainment of the state of being an object. "The meaning is the same": the sense is that there is a perception of the two dissimilar [states] involving the instigation (*preṣaṇa*), and the abandonment of that [instigation] when they are similar.

Regarding the phrase "there, in the third": the sense is that for the first and second [levels], because they lack the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is no possibility of such a statement at all. Regarding "even when the action is the same": this means together with the first level (*kakṣyā*). Regarding "taking the second": this should be understood as referring to the restriction against deficiency or excess in the rule *aṇau yā kriyā saiva cet* ("if that very action which exists in the non-causative [root]..."). However, if it were intended merely to exclude excess, then since that [restriction] would be possible even by taking the first level, [the author] provides an example where the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*) with the words beginning with "in this way" (*evam*).

Having thus explained the process where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased, he speaks regarding the process where the instigation is superimposed (*adhyāropita*), saying "or else" (*yadvā*). Regarding the phrase "due to the superimposition of causality": here too, the sole motive is the desire to express ease (*saukarya*). The sense is that it is established by experience that ease is perceived even through the abandonment of one portion of the instigation and the superimposition of another instigation. "The meaning is as before" means that in the two final stages which serve as the examples, there is an absence of the manifestation of the portion of instigation in both positions.
[Commentary] "Merely the attainment of the status of being an object" means: from that which expresses an operation (*vyāpāra*) having the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as that [object].
Regarding the phrase "the state of being less or more": the sense is that because there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), the particle *eva* excludes both [possibilities].
Since the particle *eva* here is intended to exclude connection with something else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), he says: "more."

Thus, even in the view of those who maintain that the state of being without the causative suffix (*aṇyantāvasthā*) must be understood as one and the same due to proximity in both sentences, there is no fault. However, the exclusion of "mere deficiency" (*nyūnatvamātra*) is not stated, because such a case is impossible; furthermore, since the Sūtra would be unavoidable in the second stage where the causative force (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed, it would result in the redundancy of the exclusionary sentence.

Since both the action culminating in the object (*karmaniṣṭhaphala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*) in the state of being an object (*karmatvāvasthā*), even though intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*) denote two components, it is stated that "only an excess" (*adhikya-mātram*) is excluded; thus, this alone is logical. [Commentary omitted] Regarding the phrase "because of excess" (*ādhikyāt*): in this view, by the rule *ṇau cetsā kriyā*, only an excess is excluded, not even a deficiency (*nyūnatvam*). Otherwise, it would not apply even in the third stage (*kakṣyā*), because a deficiency would be certain due to the abandonment of the portion consisting of the instigation (*preṣaṇāṃśa*) inherent in the base form (*prakṛti*). This is the intended meaning.

Why is it stated "after *ṇi*"? [To ensure] that it does not apply to the form *ārohanti*, where the causative force (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased. Nor should it be argued that because the word "*ṇau*" is heard in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the rule "if after *ṇi*," the operation will apply only to *ṇi*; for the word "*aṇau*" is also heard [in the same rule]. Furthermore, the word "*ṇeḥ*" must necessarily be stated for the sake of the subsequent rule; therefore, it is mentioned here for the sake of clarity. Why is the section beginning with "that which is the object in *aṇi*" and ending with "if it is the agent in *ṇi*" stated? [To ensure] that it does not apply to the second stage (*kakṣyā*) in the view where the causative force is superimposed (*adhyāropita-preṣaṇa-pakṣa*). Why is it stated "that which is the object in *aṇi*, if it is the agent in *ṇi*"? [To ensure] that it does not apply to the third stage in the view where the causative force has ceased (*nivṛtta-preṣaṇa-pakṣa*).
In the aphorism, three meanings of the sentence are presented and two positions are illustrated;
furthermore, four stages and three [stages] for each of the two positions have been set forth.
The third [vowel] of the first [group] is indeed barred by the third;
but the second of the second [group] is barred by the second—this is the summary.

As for the verse in the *Māghakāvya*, "The female elephant causes the rider to mount," that is established by the rule *ṇicaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74). It is not, however, the subject matter of the present sūtra (*hetumati ca*), because it takes the form of the second stage (*kakṣyā*) involving superimposed instigation (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇa*). By this, the verse "He, free from pride, constantly shows his kin as if they were masters" is explained. His kin see him; he shows them to themselves. Or alternatively: people see the kin as if they were masters; he, however, shows them [to himself].
In both cases, the ātmanepada suffix is applied by the rule "ṇicaśca" alone, and not by the present sūtra; such is the general direction.

[Commentary] Even though the term *aṇau* is explicitly heard in the rule, just as when it is said, "If there is a bridegroom residing in Vārāṇasī who is in Mathurā, then the marriage shall take place," the status of being the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the marriage is understood to belong to Mathurā alone, and not to Vārāṇasī despite its being explicitly mentioned; likewise, when it is stated, "The action that exists in the non-causative (*aṇau*) state, if that same action exists in the causative (*ṇau*) state, and that which was the object (*karman*) in the former is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the latter," the status of being the locus for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is understood to belong only to the causative base, and not to the non-causative base. Therefore, he says: "Furthermore... (*kiṃ ca*).

[The commentary is omitted. Here, this should be noted: although it has not been stated in any authoritative source that the word *karma* here refers to action (*kriyā*), nevertheless, because it is logical, consistent with the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali), and because there is no subverting evidence, it is stated as such here.

An Introduction to the Examination of the Views of Kaiyaṭa and Others: Having realized that almost all the works of the ancients on this subject are generally lax, I have exercised a degree of independence; may this be forgiven by the wise.

A restatement of the views of Kaiyaṭa and his commentators is as follows: In this sūtra, by the rule "if that which is the object in the *aṇ* [root] is the same [object] in the *ṇi*-caused [root]," the exclusion of a different object is effected; it is not, however, established that the object of the *aṇ* becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *ṇi*-caused [root], because its status as an agent is established by a separate statement, namely, "he is the agent" (*sa kartā*). This is because it is impossible for a single entity to simultaneously possess both the status of agent and object within a single action.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the Bhāṣya statement, "The king causes his servants to see [himself]," because the object consisting of the servants does exist; for the intent [of the rule] is to exclude an object other than those which are the agent and the object in the case of the root without the *ṇic* affix (*aṇau*). And in this matter, the aforementioned Bhāṣya itself is the authority. Thus, Kaiyaṭa has stated that the counter-example, "The thicket of forest bushes causes him (the cuckoo) to remember himself," is appropriate even though the cuckoo is the object [in the causative].

This has been refined by the commentators as follows: the term *kartari* (in the locative) is carried over from the previous rule and is transformed into the nominative; and since both *yaḥ* and *yacca* (which becomes *yat* by the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavacanam*) are present, there is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) based on the neuter gender. Consequently, there is no fault even when the object is simultaneously the agent (*karmakartṛ*) in the case of roots not having the suffix *ṇi*. In this way, the usage of Māgha—*kareṇurārohayate niṣādinam* ("the female elephant causes the rider to mount")—is also justified. [Commentary: The point is that the status of being the object (*karmatva*) is established in relation to the suffix *ṇi*; thus, only those roots that have two objects (*dvikarmaka*) in the base form (*aṇau*) can possibly serve as examples here.

Regarding the phrase "because of the demonstration of agency": the sense is that in the rule *aṇau yatkarma sa karttā* ("that which is the object in the causal [verb] is the agent [in the non-causal]"), since it is a general principle (*autsargikatva*) that the predicated property (*vidheya*) must be construed with the delimitor of the scope of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), the prescription of agency delimited by the status of being an object (*karmatva*) serves to demonstrate the existence of the object. Therefore, it is impossible to claim that the purpose of this rule is merely the exclusion of other objects. Here, the following must be said:

For Kaiyaṭa and others who describe [the matter] in this way, all the passages of the Bhāṣya and Vārttika located within the present sūtra are contradicted. For in the first section, it is established that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the example "the elephant, being mounted, causes the men to mount the ground," because the object (*karman*), namely "the men," exists [and thus the condition for the rule is not met]. In the second section, when the objection is raised that the result is already established by virtue of the agent being simultaneously the object (*karmakartṛtva*), it is stated that the rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) in order to exclude the application of *yak* and *ciṇ*.
However, in the third section, it is stated that this sūtra is intended for cases where the state (*bhāva*) resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*).
Among these, the first is contradictory, because humans possess agency over their own atoms (*aṇu*).

The second is also contradictory, because according to your own reasoning, the status of being "like an object" (*karmavadbhāva*) does not even exist [in this case]. For the *Vārttika* states: "The rule 'like an object' applies to intransitive verbs. For this very reason, the third [alternative] is also not tenable.

[Commentary]: "Because the atom (aṇu) possesses the status of an agent" means that you intend to express precisely the absence of any object other than the agent and the [primary] object. Now, one might object: "In this case, there is an additional object consisting of the 'place' (sthala). Its root state is the non-causative (aṇyantāvasthā) condition: *manuṣyā ārohayamāṇaṃ hastinam ārohanti* ('the men mount the elephant being mounted'). This is done by increasing the aspect of the result (*phalāṃśavṛddhi*) in order to express that very [action], just as there is an increase in instigation (*preraṇāvṛddhi*) for the sake of expressing an excellence of facility; thus, it is made a transitive verb with two objects (*dvikarmaka*). And so, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the upward location, the object situated therein, and the activity conducive to the conjunction of both."

By the word *sthala*, the wooden seat situated on the back of an elephant is meant. As for the phrase "the elephant-keepers mount the elephant," this is merely an illustration of the root form of the term *ārohayamāṇa*; the portion ending in *ārohayamāṇa* is presented as an example of the grammatical rule (*sūtra*) for the sake of providing a concrete instance. The word "elephant" (*hastī*) applies to both [the agent and the object] according to the "middle jewel" (*madhyamaṇi*) maxim.

If it is argued that the intention of the first section is that just as the *ātmanepada* arises there [in the case of *ārohayate hastī svayameva*], so too should it arise here [in the case of *ārohayante manuṣyāḥ sthalam*]—no; for this contradicts the commentary on that [passage], which aims to demonstrate the state of the causative (*ṇic*) based on the root [of *ruh*] in the sentence "men ascend the dry land" (*manuṣyāḥ sthalamārohanti*).
Or rather, from this very lack of satisfaction [with the previous solution], he says: "The second [alternative] also...

And thus, since the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply in the case of a transitive verb (*sakarmaka*), the contradiction with the middle [section] regarding the statement "it is established by that" is indeed clear. P.

Now, it might be argued that [the result] is established by virtue of being a "subject that is also an object" (*karmakartṛ*) because, in the third stage where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) has been superimposed, there is an absence of "equality of action" with the action residing in the object within the same verbal root; thus, the rule for behaving like an object (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply. However, this is incorrect. Why? Because in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), by reason of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), one must understand that the behavior like an object applies when the action residing in the object is equal to the action of that very subject who behaves like an object within that same verbal root. If you say this, we reply: No.

Adopting the position that the causal impulsion (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased, since its occurrence is possible [in that state], when the meaning "the elephant becomes submissive" is understood, the meaning "someone makes the elephant submissive" also necessarily appears. Consequently, when only the words expressive of that meaning are presented, there is no determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether "this one alone should be accepted" or "this one not. For there is no evidence that a usage based on two alternative positions must be explained by adopting only one of those positions; such is the intention, as explained at length elsewhere.

"For this very reason, [it is] not so. The meaning is that precisely because the status of being an object (*karman*) is not attained, even the third section is not contradictory for you. Furthermore, in this case, the forgetting of the subject matter (*uddeśya*) would follow; thus, this is a great oversight even on the part of the great scholars. Moreover, a sentence intended to exclude other objects would be entirely fruitless, as examples [of such cases] are difficult to find. For there is no object distinct from those which are the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) in the *aṇ* [verbal root] that could possibly exist in the *ṇi* [causative], such that it might be excluded by this [rule].

As for what Jayāditya stated: "The inclusion of the word *sa-* (with) is for the sake of excluding other actions; [as in] 'the elephant-keepers mount the elephant,' whereas 'the mounting elephant causes the men to mount the dry land.'"

His intention was that, by taking the unity [of the agent] through the *ṇic* suffix, since the *ṇi* is absent within the base of the *śānac* suffix, the elephant (*hastin*)—which is the object (*karman*)—becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the meaning of the *ṇij*-derived form which serves as the base for the *tiṅ* suffix; however, this too is not correct, because the point is already established by the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). For there are two *ṇic* suffixes here. In the first case, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) has already been applied, as in "ārohayamāṇa. But in the second case, since the ground (*sthala*), which is the object in the non-*ṇij* form (*aṇau karmaṇaḥ*), does not become the agent in the *ṇij*-form, there is no possibility [for the application of the rule] at all.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*): this is stated according to the method of the commentaries of those who explain that humans ascend onto dry land, which aims to demonstrate the final state of the root action (*mūla-ṇyanta*).

Regarding the inclusion of the term "that which" (*yat*): when the meaning is "if that which is the object (*karman*) in the root [action] becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative (*ṇic*)," its acquisition occurs by way of restriction according to the aforementioned method. Furthermore, based on Rudra’s lexicon (*rudrakośa*), which states, "The word *karman* is considered to mean 'that which is pervaded' (*vyāpya*) and 'action' (*kriyā*), and is used in both the masculine and neuter genders," the word *karman* can also be masculine.

Now, one might object: "In the state without the causative suffix (aṇ), as in 'men ascend the dry land' (*sthalam ārohanti manuṣyāḥ*), since the object (*karman*)—the dry land—does not possess the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative (*ṇic*) state, how can there be an application [of the rule] here? To this, he says: "By virtue of being a *ṇit*."

The meaning is that since there is no possibility [of the rule applying] at all, it is appropriate to understand by the word *aṇau* (in the non-causative) the very root-form in its non-causative state (*aṇyantamūla*) which serves as the example for the causative (*ṇyantamūla*), because of its fixed presence. Furthermore, it should be understood that by taking them as identical through their shared *ṇi*-characteristic, and because the status of the object in the non-causative becomes the agent in the causative is established elsewhere, one could also claim that an action-object distinct from the non-causative object exists in every instance; thus, the application of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would not arise in the case of *ārohayamāṇa*.

[Commentary omitted] As for that which was cited by Haradatta—namely, "the elephant-keepers mount the elephant; the elephant makes them mount"—that too is not correct. For this is the form belonging to the second stage (*kakṣyā*) in the view where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed (*adhyāropita*). And in that case, there is simply no identity of action (*samānakriyatva*), because the causative suffix (*ṇic*) introduces a different operation. If one asks, "What follows from this?"—bear in mind that this would contradict your own treatise. For the text of Jayāditya states: "The mention of *ṇau* (in the causative) is for the sake of [establishing] identity of action."

The commentary of Haradatta states that in the rule *ṇau ced* (Pāṇini 1.3.67), one must carry over the phrase *aṇau yat* from the previous sūtra and interpret it as follows: "If the very same entity that was expressed in the *aṇ* [denominative base] is to be expressed in the *ṇi*-causative, then [the causative suffix applies]. This is so that the rule may apply only when there is no difference in the action inherent in the verbal root itself, and not when there is a difference in action characterized by the relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*).

Consequently, since the purpose is already served by this interpretation, the statement of Jayāditya—"the inclusion of the word *yat* is for the sake of excluding other objects"—as well as the commentaries of those who explained him, are clearly rendered devoid of scope.

[Commentary] "The absence of an object (*nirviṣayitā*) is indeed clear. Since the prevention of the *ātmanepada* ending is already established by Haradatta’s statement and the statement in the *Vṛtti* that "the inclusion of the word 'with' (*sa-*) is for the purpose of excluding other actions," it would follow that the sentence intended to convey the identity of the action (*samānakriyatva*) is redundant. Nor can it be argued that in that context the word "action" (*kriyā*) refers to the verbal root (*dhātu*), such that the rule would not apply when there is a difference in roots; for just as in the case of the rule "like the object" (*karmavat karmaṇā*), this rule also has the capacity to prevent application when there is a difference in roots through the very principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

It should also be understood that this is because the stage formed by the integration of different *dhātus* lacks that as its root. [Commentary omitted]. As for what was stated by Jayāditya—"What is the purpose of [specifying] 'agent'? [Consider: *hastipakā ārohanti hastinam*, *tān ārohayati mahāmātraḥ*" (The elephant-keepers mount the elephant; the mahout makes them mount)—that too is refuted by this very argument.

Furthermore, the deliberation by Haradatta on this point—claiming that the rule will not apply simply because there exists another object (*karman*)—is entirely in vain, since according to the aforementioned reasoning, such an example cannot possibly occur. This is the general direction [of the argument]. [This concludes] the refutation of the views of the *Prakriyākaumudī* and its commentators.

(1) A restatement of the view of the *Prakriyākaumudī* and its refutation: As for what was explained by the ancients as a single syntactical unit—namely, "if that which is the object (*karman*) in the *aṇ*-stem is itself the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *ṇi*-stem"—that is not correct, because it results in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the second stage (*kakṣyā*) in the case of superimposed instigation (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇa*). [Commentary]: "By the aforementioned method" means that there is an absence of identity of action (*samānakriyatva*). "Because of over-extension to the second stage" should also be understood to mean that, according to my own method of interpretation, there is over-extension even to the examples cited in the Bhāṣya within the first section.

(2) A translation of the *Prasāda*, a commentary on the *Prakriyākaumudī*, and its refutation: Although the author of the *Prasāda* has dissected sections such as "that which is the object in the root [verb]" (*aṇau yat karma*) and so forth, and interpreted the root text by breaking it down in accordance with the words of Jayāditya, Kaiyaṭa, and others, nevertheless, because the root itself is incorrect, total error is unavoidable.
(3) A translation of the commentary on the *Prakriyākaumudī* known as the *Prakāśa*.

Furthermore, regarding what those who explain the earlier text by means of refuting the *Prasāda* have said—that the Bhāṣyakāra did not adopt the sentence-meaning "the mention of *aṇau* is for the sake of [specifying] the same action" because there is no purpose [for it]—it is as follows: the *ātmanepada* occurs after a *ṇi*-caused root.

When it is stated, "if that which is the object in *aṇau* is the agent in *ṇau*," this is understood through proximity (*pratyāsatti*) as follows: by whichever *ṇic* the *ātmanepada* is intended to be prescribed after the *ṇi*-caused form, by that very same *ṇic*, in the case of the non-*ṇi*-caused base root (*prakṛti*) from which that *ṇic* is derived, if that which was the object is indeed the agent, then [the *ātmanepada* applies] in that very same *ṇi*-caused form.

Consequently, just as in the example "the elephant-keepers mount the elephant; the mounting elephant makes them mount" (and "he sprinkles those who are afraid with urine"), there is no [application of the rule] despite the difference in verbal roots (*dhātu*), so too there will be none here despite the difference in the relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*). For this very reason, the third interpretation of the sentence-meaning was disregarded by the Teachers (*ācārya*) because it is not supported by the *Bhāṣya*; for the unity of the single sentence—expressed as "if that very [agent] is the agent of the causative form" (*ṇyanta*)—is naturally perceived.

Thus, the two-fold description of the sentence-meaning proposed by the ancients—based on the assumptions of ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and the connection of separated elements (*vyavahitānvaya*)—is unacceptable, as it results in the assumption of multiple purposeless and strained interpretations. Furthermore, in this view, the inclusion of the term *ṇau* (in the locative case) would be redundant; for if that were absent, the connection would occur through a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) based on the statement "that which is the object under the *aṇ* [affix] becomes the agent," and consequently, the exclusion of other objects (*karmāntara-nivṛtti*) would not be achieved. Therefore, the inclusion of *ṇau* must necessarily be made, as it brings about a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) that serves to exclude other objects.
[Commentary] "Having broken" (*bhaṅktvā*): the meaning is that there is also an interpretation intended to exclude other [types of] actions.

"Thus, having employed" (*evaṃ prayojya*): it is clear in his work that therefore there is no fault in the third stage of the position where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed. "The meaning of the second sentence" (*dvitīyavākyārtha*): the meaning is that it is constituted by the identity of action (*sāmānakriyatva*).

[Supplementation: [The supplementation] of the phrase "the object to be established" and so forth. [Distant connection: The distant element *yad* in *aṇau yad* is connected with *cet* in *ṇau cet*. [End of commentary. (4) Refutation of the *Prakāśa* commentary.
To this, the following must be said:

It is unproven that the author of the Bhāṣya did not accept [this]. For it is only by relying on the view that the words for "action" (*karman*) found in the Bhāṣya refer to "activity" (*kriyā*), whereas in the sentence "if there were an agent" (*kartā cet*) they refer to "factors of action" (*kāraka*), that an interpretation of the Bhāṣya is appropriate. Otherwise, the entire body of the Bhāṣya up to the conclusion of the Sūtras would fall into the error of being unintelligible.

As for what was stated, beginning with "due to the absence of purpose" and ending with "it will not occur," that is due to excessive haste. For when the causal suffix (*ṇic*) is superimposed upon the non-causal root (*aṇ*), the elephant is the object (*karman*) in that [non-causal] state, and it is clearly the same [elephant] that becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in that very [causal] state. Therefore, how can there be an exclusion of that [agenthood] by means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*)? And where does the distinction between the instigated (*prayojya*) and the instigator (*prayojaka*) reside?

If it is argued, "We maintain that there is an addition of the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*)," what follows from that? For by this much alone, the agent (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative form (*aṇau*) does not become the object (*karma*) in the causative form (*ṇau*) [rather, it is the object in the non-causative that becomes the agent in the causative]. Furthermore, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is highly dissimilar, because the two causative suffixes (*ṇic*) derived from the roots *ruha* and *hi* are different in that context.

Moreover, having stated that the syntactic unity is natural due to the perception of a single sentence, to then say that the inclusion of the phrase "if in the causative" (*ṇau cet*) results in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) that excludes other objects—that too is clearly self-contradictory.
If it is argued that this was accepted out of necessity (*agatyā*), we say no; for its fruitlessness has already been stated.
Regarding the phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*): this has been demonstrated previously.
Regarding the question "from where [does it come]? (*kutratyaśca*): the sense is that they have spoken thus only in the context of the position that [the self] is superimposed (*adhyāropita*).
"Mutually contradictory"—this alone is the essential refutation here.

Regarding "fruitlessness": since examples such as *sthalam ārohayati* (he causes to mount onto dry land) are already excluded by the very fact that there is no identity of action (*samānakriyatva*), [the objection is redundant]. If it is argued, "We speak thus in accordance with Kaiyaṭa and others," then the author of the *Prasāda* has likewise dismantled the root text in accordance with Jayāditya, the author of the *Nyāsa*, Haradatta, and others. What wrong has he done?
Therefore, it remains established that the works of everyone from Kaiyaṭa down to the moderns are entirely flawed in this regard.

The final conclusion, however, has indeed been established in accordance with the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali). It might be argued as follows: the primary examples concern the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*); yet the core of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), as settled in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and other works, is that there is no application of the rule of "acting like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) because the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakriyatva*). Thus, since the status of being non-transitive (*akarmakatva*) is necessary for both the example and the counter-example, the use of the term "object" (*karman*) in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and so forth, would be untenable. Yet it is seen: in the *Bhāṣya*, "the king causes his servants to see himself" (*darśayate bhṛtyān rājā*); and in the *Bhāṣya* and *Vṛtti*, "the thicket of the forest causes him to remember itself" (*smarayatyenaṃ vanagulmaḥ svayameva*)."

If it is asked, "What is its [the *ṇic* affix's] status?"—to this they reply: "The object (*karman*) is not intended to be expressed here. Their intention is as follows: In the case of the expression "a hamlet on a deep river" (*gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), even though there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the bank after the cognition of the non-difference between the meanings of the words "deep" (*gabhīra*) and "river" (*nadī*), the word "deep" retains its significance by taking into account the initial cognition. Similarly here, in the second stage under the view that the causative force (*preṣaṇā*) is superimposed, once the object has been construed with the meaning of the *ṇic*, then upon the abandonment of the object—just as in the case of the meaning of the *ṇic* itself—the *ṇic* affix and the word for the object (*karma-pada*) are both abandoned.

There is purposefulness by taking the primary cognition [of the literal meaning] as a basis, because it is accepted that *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is a relation with that which is to be made known (*jñāpya*). And here, what is to be made known takes the form of the qualified meaning of the sentence. This very same process is the way indication functions toward excellence (*prāśastya*) in the case of an *arthavāda*. That indeed is the method for explaining established [texts]. However, since the employment of words is within one’s own control, it is more appropriate to employ [words] entirely free from [the constraints of] ritual action; such is the direction of the argument.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "in summary" (*niṣkarṣa*): this refers to the passage beginning with "according to my method" (*madrītyā*).
Regarding the phrase "taking the initial cognition" (*prāthamikabodhamādāya*): it should also be understood as meaning "by way of grasping the intention (*tātparya*) of the definition.
Regarding the phrase "possessing purposefulness" (*sārthakya*): the meaning is "the purposefulness of its application" (*prayogasārthakya*).

Regarding the rule *ṇicaḥ karmapadasya ca*: since there must necessarily be the removal of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense that "it becomes the object of knowledge," so too, for the production of the causative suffix, there must necessarily be an understanding—intended for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)—that the instigation has as its object an activity not desired by the servant which is conducive to [the king's] seeing. It is with this intention that the word *enam* (him) is employed; such is the underlying meaning.

Regarding the phrase "svājñeyeti": the meaning is the relationship between the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) as understood from the words. The sense is that there is an indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the meaning "becoming the object of the king's vision" (which is connected to the primary meaning of the sentence expressing an instigation by the king directed toward the servant)—namely, the meaning "becoming the object of the king's vision. [The commentary is omitted. By abandoning [the literal meanings of] the servant and so forth, by adopting pure non-difference, and by resorting to the fact that the ritual action (karma) is for that purpose, the wise one shall cross over [to liberation].

All of this has been sounded at the very root. Let us now follow the subject at hand. Regarding the statement "he remembers the forest thicket," the forms *smarayati enam* (he causes him to remember) are employed in the Bhāṣya and the Vṛtti; and it has already been stated that this is intended according to the primary understanding [of the meaning]. That too occurs only under the view where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed, because in any other view, the status of the cuckoo as the object (*karman*) would be impossible.

Although, according to the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), only those roots whose general meaning is "knowledge" (*jñāna*) are included—and since the root *smṛ* here has a specific meaning—it would be difficult to establish the status of the cuckoo as the object (*karman*) even there, as it is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative form (*aṇau*); nevertheless, by the force of this very Bhāṣya, it should be understood that the root *smṛ* is also included in the rule *gatibuddhi*.

[Commentary: Regarding "of the servants, etc. (*bhṛtyādīnām*): examples such as *darśayate bhṛtyān rājā* ("The king shows his servants") consist of forms where the object resides in the actual referent (*lakṣyastha*).
Regarding "pure non-difference" (*śuddhābheda*): the meaning is that absolute non-difference in sense is accepted with respect to the second stage (*kakṣyā*).

"Of the sentence regarding the object" (*karmavākyasya*) means: of a sentence composed of an object that serves as an illustration. "By resorting to its being for that purpose" (*tādarthyāśrayaṇāt*) means: by resorting to its being for the sake of the primary cognition.
"In this case, a particular... (*iha viśeṣa*) means: a particular consisting of recollection preceded by longing. [The commentary is omitted.]
